g_cea35522149d:
The page tree, in pure functions.
*
Nothing here touches the disk: these functions take an index and return a
new one. That is what makes ordering, moves and cascading deletes testable
in a few milliseconds, with no database and no browser.
*
Order among siblings is a plain number. Inserting between two neighbours
takes the midpoint, which avoids rewriting the whole sibling list on every
drag. A floating-point number eventually runs out of precision after some
fifty insertions at the same spot: when the gap becomes too small,
`renumber` reassigns clean integers to the sibling list. The case is rare,
but it happens, and it is silently destructive if ignored.

g_d880264f7dff:
Nook's design tokens.

One place defines a value. The colours use `light-dark()`: the light value
and the dark value live side by side, and `color-scheme` decides. One
important consequence: the theme follows the system from the first pixel
painted, with no JavaScript.

That is a constraint, not a preference — the product's CSP forbids inline
scripts, so the usual trick of a small anti-flash script in the <head> is
impossible here. Switching manually is done by setting `data-theme` on
<html>, which does nothing but redefine `color-scheme`.

BlockNote exposes its colours as CSS variables. We redefine them from our
own tokens, for both schemes at once: our tokens already switch between
light and dark on their own, so pointing both at the same variables is
enough and saves maintaining two palettes.

We touch only colours, radii and typography. The editor's behaviours — drag
handle, slash menu, multi-block selection — stay the library's: rewriting
them would produce exactly the wobbly affordances we are trying to avoid.

g_f8982dc234cc:
Debounced autosave.
*
There is no "Save" button in Nook, so this module carries the promise of
losing nothing. Three moments matter, and forgetting them is the usual way
to lose the last paragraph written:
*
  - after a pause in typing (the common case);
  - when the tab goes to the background or closes, because a pending timer
    will never fire;
  - on unmount, typically when changing page.
*
On failure, the changes go back into the queue rather than being thrown
away: the next keystroke will retry, and the state moves to `error` so the
interface can say so.
